guest: Chris Auth / Kevin Fischer / Tyler Osborn / Pushkar Ranade（Intel）等
summary: Dwarkesh 参观 Intel 先进晶圆厂并访谈工艺、封装与 CTO：AI 需求冲击、14A 良率闭环、High-NA 经济性、IDM→Foundry 的 PDK 陡坡、Foveros/hybrid bonding 节距演进、EUV 工具瓶颈与 CapEx–客户结构悖论。理解「GPU 荒」背后的制造约束地图。

> **免责声明：** 本文是基于 Dwarkesh Podcast《What will computer chips look like in 2045?》（2026 年 10 月 22 日发布，YouTube 约 69 分钟）的 AI 中文精读改写，非官方翻译。整理依据为节目页随附官方转写（带说话人）；正式引用请以原音视频与官方文字稿为准。

## 这期在聊什么

AI 训练与推理对先进制程算力的需求，正在给半导体制造带来「前所未见」的冲击。Dwarkesh Patel 花两天时间参观 Intel 最先进的晶圆厂，并与工艺开发、先进封装与 CTO 等管理层对谈：一条新制程从实验室走到量产要经历什么、良率如何月复一月爬升、Intel 从 IDM 转向代工时 PDK 踩过哪些坑、EUV / High-NA 与供应商产能如何卡住扩产、先进封装与混合键合把「芯片之间怎么说话」推到哪一步——以及，在 TSMC 领先制程订单已被 AI 加速器（尤其 Nvidia）占满的溢出需求下，Intel 的追赶路线图究竟是什么。

嘉宾主线包括：工艺开发负责人 Chris Auth（14A / 良率与缺陷）、Kevin Fischer（18A / 18A-P 改进例会）、先进封装 Tyler Osborn（Foveros、hybrid bonding 节距）、CTO Pushkar Ranade（工具瓶颈、规模经济、CapEx）。片中还穿插 ASML 的 Peter Wennink、Applied Materials 的 Gary Dickerson 等外部声音，强调设备侧同样供不应求。标题里的「2045」不是科幻时间旅行，而是用足够长的时间尺度追问：当晶体管继续缩小、开始真正三维堆叠、封装互连逼近芯片内部金属层时，计算机硬件会变成什么样。

## 核心论点（按叙事顺序）

### 1. AI 需求是半导体制造的「量级冲击」

开场即定调：AI 对算力的指数级胃口，正在同时推高「做更多芯片」和「让每颗芯片更强」两条线。晶圆厂的真正瓶颈往往不在晶圆厂自身愿不愿意扩，而在上游光刻、沉积、量测等工具的交付节奏。ASML 相关表述被用来说明：EUV 等高端工具年产量有上限，且扩产意愿谨慎——没有设备，就谈不上在本地把先进芯片「做出来」。Peter Wennink 等人的旁白把供需差说得很直白：需求轻易高出最大产能四到五成，这种缺口在过往周期里几乎没见过。

对听者的含义是：讨论「GPU 荒」时，如果只停在 Nvidia 或云厂商下单意愿，会漏掉真正的物理约束层——工具交期、洁净室人力、以及节点切换时工具组合的可复用比例。

### 2. 新节点不是「宣布一次」，而是数年的缺陷狩猎

以 14A 为例，Chris Auth 描述：节点已开发三年以上，当前接近敲定工艺与工具集，并做逐层微调。良率提升不是玄学：产线内量测（inline metrology）先抓晶圆上的缺陷点，终端再靠电测 / 分选闭环；每个月能改的是「定位—归因—改工艺或改工具」的循环速度。Dwarkesh 追问得很细：假设本月有一条 14A 线在跑，到下个月良率变好，中间到底发生了什么？答案几乎总是同一套：找到缺陷来源，改配方或改机台参数，再验证是否引入新缺陷。

Intel 也用 10nm 节点当年延误的代价，提醒「激进节点跳跃」与「可交付进度」之间的权衡有多贵。对外部观察者来说，这解释了为什么「宣布 N+1 节点」和「客户能稳定流片」之间常常隔着好几年新闻真空。

### 3. High-NA EUV：同一台工具，不同架构会得出不同经济结论

Dwarkesh 追问：Intel 在 14A 上采用 High-NA EUV，而 TSMC 公开表示现阶段经济性不足。Auth 的解释关键在架构差异——例如 backside power 减轻正面节距压力，使 High-NA 在自家路线上更「划算」。要点不是「谁更爱新工具」，而是：制程架构决定工具组合的 ROI，没有放之四海皆准的采购清单。

这也是理解「技术领先」与「成本领先」为何经常分叉的钥匙：同样一台 ASML 机器，放进不同的金属层/供电/晶体管故事里，曝光次数、多重图案化复杂度与缺陷密度会完全不同，于是「值不值得上 High-NA」变成公司私有的会计题，而不是行业公论。

### 4. 从 IDM 到 Foundry：PDK 是文化与工程的双重陡坡

公开报道曾提到 18A PDK 问题影响外部客户设计。Auth 坦承：做了几十年 IDM，产品团队看晶体管数据的方式，和给外部客户交付「可综合、可验证、指令都可用」的 PDK，是两套肌肉。竞争对手也曾走过这条学习曲线。Dwarkesh 补刀：历史上 Intel 产线主要做自家芯片，而 TSMC 服务多客户带来更多晶圆学习样本、更多收入再投入、更强的交期压力——这可能是代工优势的结构性来源之一。

节目没有把 Intel 描写成「已经赢了代工转型」，而是更接近一份体检报告：工艺可以接近球园区，但 foundry 产品（PDK、支持、可预测性）才是外部客户肯不敢把旗舰 AI 芯片押上来的门槛。

### 5. 存储、逻辑与热：为什么 HBM 式堆叠不能简单搬到逻辑上

中段有一段关于堆叠的物理课：逻辑比存储更耗电、更热，因此不能像 HBM 或 3D NAND 那样轻易做很高的 DRAM 式堆叠。长期限制是热，而不是「会不会 3D」。这为后文「先进封装」埋下伏笔——既然不能把所有东西竖着堆成一座逻辑塔，就把异构芯片在封装层密密地「焊」在一起，用互连密度换系统带宽。

### 6. 先进封装：把「芯片怎么互连」变成和晶体管同等重要的战场

节目后半把视角从「晶体管层」拉到 packaging：从传统并排放置，到 2.5D / 3D 堆叠，再到 hybrid bonding 把互连节距从百微米级压到数十乃至亚十微米。Tyler Osborn 谈到 Foveros 量产约 25μm 节距、实验室已到 sub-10，并展望若封装节距逼近后端金属层尺寸，几乎可以把部分上层金属「挪」到封装互连上。对 AI 而言，这意味着：算力墙之后，下一堵墙往往是内存带宽与 chiplet 之间的通信密度；封装不再是「出货前的工序」，而是性能规格本身。

Osborn 还提到非 AI 的客户端场景也可能受益——例如 CPU 与相关芯片之间的原始互连密度。换句话说，先进封装不是只服务训练集群的奢侈品，而可能重新定义消费级 SoC 的拆分方式。

### 7. 供应商瓶颈、工具复用与 CapEx 现实

Pushkar Ranade 承认：ASML EUV 年产量有限是硬约束，但不是唯一瓶颈——几乎每类关键工具都紧。应对方式是节点间尽量保持工具可复用（例如 18A→14A 约八成工具集可延续），并把已装机台的产出率挖尽。规模经济方面，TSMC 领先制程出货量可达 Intel 数倍；追赶既要工艺「在正确球园区且可预测」，也要规模慢慢长。CapEx 对比被直接摆上台面：TSMC 年 CapEx 量级约 500 亿美元、Intel 约 200 亿——而现在买下的工具，将决定谁能接住下一波 AI 溢出需求。Ranade 的回应是：今天对比不公平，因为对方几乎是「全世界的代工」，Intel 仍主要是「Intel 的代工」；成为外部客户的 foundry 之后，CapEx 才会跟上来。

这段对「主权算力 / 本地建厂」讨论也很刺耳：钱可以批，但工具、人才与良率学习曲线买不来加速键；而 incumbent 之所以极度风险厌恶，是因为停产一天的美元成本高到没人愿意做大胆实验。

### 8. 收束：溢出需求是机会，但扩产是风险厌恶行业里的慢变量

结尾回到开场问题：面对已到且仍在加速的 AI 需求，Intel 该做什么？讨论指向——在工具与人员已是瓶颈的前提下，更关键的是把现有产线良率、PDK 可用性、封装与客户导入做成「可被外部设计团队信任」的产品；盲目赌一座新厂，对任何 incumbent 都过于危险。Dwarkesh 用「TSMC N3 上 AI 加速器已占多数、其中 Nvidia 可能独占大半」来刻画溢出：CPU 与其他负载仍需要先进产能，这正是第二供应商的窗口——但窗口只对「交得出、料号稳、文档齐」的工厂打开。

## 值得记住的几句话（意译）

- AI 对半导体制造的冲击，是「做更多」与「做更强」同时发生，而真正卡脖子的经常是上游工具。
- 良率爬坡 = 缺陷定位闭环的速度，不是口号。
- High-NA 等新工具的经济性，取决于你的晶体管/供电架构，而不是工具白皮书。
- IDM 肌肉 ≠ Foundry 肌肉；PDK 是转代工的试金石。
- 逻辑太热，不能照搬 HBM 式堆叠；系统带宽会更多押在先进封装上。
- 封装节距逼近后端金属层时，系统性能的定义会改写。
- CapEx 与客户结构绑定：先成为「别人的工厂」，再谈与 TSMC 同量级的资本开支。

## 谁该看 / 怎么看

- **做 infra / 投资半导体与 AI 算力**：整期几乎是「先进制程 + 封装」速成课，建议全听。
- **做模型/应用、只关心 GPU 供给**：可精听开场需求冲击、Ranade 的瓶颈与 CapEx、以及封装与互连相关段落。
- **对 Intel 股价叙事过敏者**：把它当产业纪录片而非投资建议；节目大量技术细节，少有短线结论。
- **时间不够**：优先 Auth 的良率闭环 + Osborn 的封装节距 + Ranade 的工具/CapEx 三段，约能覆盖 80% 决策相关信息。

# 详细解读：当 AI 撞上晶圆厂——Intel 厂访里的瓶颈地图

## 一、为什么这期是本周「算力基建」议题的必听

大多数 AI 访谈停在模型能力、产品发布与云厂商资本开支数字；这期把镜头直接推进洁净室。它回答的不是「明年算力够不够」的情绪题，而是一组更硬的工程题：先进节点如何爬良率、代工转型卡在哪份文档、EUV 工具一年能产多少台、封装节距还能量几个数量级、以及「第二供应商」叙事在物理世界上是否站得住。

若你的工作依赖 GPU/加速器供给、云厂商 CapEx、主权算力政策，或只是想理解为什么「有钱也买不到算力」，这期提供的是把新闻标题翻译回约束条件的词典。Dwarkesh 的提问风格偏「工程师旁听会」：他会追问本月良率到下月良率之间到底改了什么，而不是满足于「我们正在 Progress」类表述——因此适合当作产业纪录片精读，而不是股价催化剂解读。

与同周其他访谈相比，它的稀缺性在于**同时覆盖工艺、代工产品化、工具供应链、先进封装四层**；通常这四层会拆成四场垂直会议。把它们缝在一集里，反而更容易看到层级之间的耦合：例如 PDK 不行时，再好的 High-NA 故事也换不成外部客户晶圆；封装节距上不去时，再先进的晶体管也喂不饱 HBM 带宽故事。

## 二、背景：三条并行的产业故事线

**故事线 A：需求侧失控式扩张。** 训练与推理同时扩张，先进制程上的 AI 加速器占比快速抬升。节目引用的外部声音（设备商、光刻商）把缺口描述为「高出最大产能 40–50%」量级——这不是常规半导体周期的库存调节，更像一次结构冲击。Dwarkesh 开场就强调：从未见过对半导体制造如此大的冲击。对听众而言，这意味着把「GPU 荒」理解为单一公司产能问题已经不够；它是整条工具—晶圆—封装链的共振。

**故事线 B：供应侧是工具网络，不是单一工厂。** 晶圆厂扩产受制于 ASML、应用材料等上游；EUV 年产量有上限，且厂商没有动力把产能曲线拉成垂直线。于是「批预算」「市长剪彩」「CHIPS 支票」都不自动等于「明年多出 N 万片」。Ranade 还指出：EUV 是更显眼的瓶颈，但不是唯一瓶颈——沉积、量测、蚀刻等几乎每类关键工具都紧。供应链的「木桶最短板」会随节点切换而移动。

**故事线 C：Intel 的双重身份危机。** 一边要在 18A / 14A 上证明工艺竞争力，一边要从 IDM 文化长出 foundry 产品能力（PDK、客户支持、可预测交期）。TSMC 用多客户学习曲线与更大体量 CapEx 拉开差距；溢出需求理论上给第二供应商窗口，但窗口只对「能被外部设计团队信任」的工厂打开。节目没有写成励志片，更像一份带细节的体检报告。

这三条线在政策讨论里经常被拧成一股「重振美国制造」口号；厂访的价值，是把口号拆回可证伪的工程变量。

## 三、逐段拆解：节目真正在论证什么

### 1. 良率闭环 = 先进制程的真实管理对象

Chris Auth 对 14A 的描述，把「制程进度」从公关时间表还原成缺陷管理系统：inline metrology + end-of-line 电测，月度改进来自归因速度。Dwarkesh 追问「从现在到下个月良率为什么会变」时，答案几乎总是同一套循环：找到缺陷 → 改工艺或改工具参数 → 验证是否引入新缺陷。

这对外部分析有三个含义：

- **看 Intel（或任何 foundry）时，应少看节点命名，多看客户能否复现良率曲线。** 命名可以超前，良率不能。
- **10nm 历史的引用不是怀旧，而是风险模型：** 过度并行、过度激进的节点跳跃，会以「年」为单位惩罚整条产品线与生态承诺。
- **「开发三年以上」这类时间尺度**，应成为评估任何「两年内国产替代先进制程」叙事的冷静剂。

结合 Kevin Fischer 出现的 18A / 18A-P 改进例会片段，还能看到大型制造组织如何把「想法」变成「可上线实验」：早会里有人提 yield/performance 点子，有人把关优先级——先进制程的日常不是灵感，是实验队列管理。

### 2. High-NA 争议是「架构会计」而不是「勇气竞赛」

TSMC 说 High-NA 现阶段不经济，Intel 说 14A 上要用——表面矛盾，Auth 用 backside power 等架构差异化解：背面供电减轻正面节距压力后，同一套光刻工具的 ROI 会改写。解读重点：

- 工具导入决策是**路径依赖**的：你的供电、金属层、多重曝光策略，决定同一台机器的边际价值。
- 媒体若把 High-NA 写成「领先/落后」二元标签，会误导；更准确的问题是：**在既定晶体管故事下，曝光成本与缺陷密度如何权衡。**
- 对投资人与政策制定者：不要把「谁先买 High-NA」当成简单的技术军备竞赛计分板。

这也解释了为什么设备商的出货节奏如此关键：工具不只是产能乘数，还是架构路线的锁定装置——你为某代节点买下的组合，会约束下一代能走多激进。

### 3. PDK：代工转型的「产品化」时刻

公开报道中的 18A PDK 问题，被节目当作 foundry 学习曲线的标本。Auth 的核心对比是：IDM 几十年里，产品团队可以靠内部关系看晶体管数据；外部客户需要的是版本化、可验证、指令完备、可综合的设计包。竞争对手也曾走过这条陡坡。

Dwarkesh 进一步提出结构性假说：历史上 Intel 产线主要服务自家芯片，而 TSMC 服务多客户——更多晶圆学习样本、更多收入再投入、更强交期压力——可能是代工优势的来源之一。这一假说无法在单集里被「证明」，但它提供了很好的观察框架：

- **工艺演示晶圆 ≠ 客户量产流片。**
- **Foundry 的产品是「可被陌生人使用的制造服务」，不是「自家 CPU 能做出性能」。**
- 若 Intel 要承接被 TSMC 挤出的非顶级 AI 加速器负载、CPU、或其他需要先进节点的设计，**第一产品往往是 PDK + 支持 SLA**，晶圆反而是交付物。

分析推论（明确非嘉宾原话）：代工转型失败模式通常不是「晶体管不行」，而是「外部团队无法低摩擦地完成从 RTL 到 GDS 再到量产的闭环」。体检应盯客户工程师的抱怨清单，而不是只盯 benchmark 海报。

### 4. 热限制如何把叙事推向封装

中段关于堆叠的物理讨论容易被当成花絮，实际上它规定了中期硬件形态：逻辑比存储更耗电、更热，不能像 HBM 或 3D NAND 那样轻易做很高的竖堆。于是系统带宽问题更多转移到异构 chiplet + 先进封装互连。

Tyler Osborn 给出可检验的节距演进：历史上第一级互连约 130–150μm，Foveros 量产约 25μm，研发已到 sub-10，并展望逼近后端金属层（约 0.5–1μm 量级）时，几乎可以把部分上层金属功能「挪」到封装互连。含义包括：

- **AI 训练集群的下一跳性能**，可能更多来自封装与内存子系统，而不是单纯节点宣传。
- **客户端/非 AI 芯片**也可能受益（CPU 与配套芯片的互连密度）——先进封装不是只服务超大集群的奢侈品。
- 当封装成为性能规格本身，「外包封装」与「自研封装」的战略权重会上升，供应链尽调必须把封装厂与 bonding 能力算进去。

### 5. CapEx、规模经济与战略悖论

Ranade 承认 TSMC 在领先制程出货规模上可达数倍优势，并强调节点间工具复用（如 18A→14A 约八成工具集可延续）与挖尽装机产出。面对「TSMC ~$50B vs Intel ~$20B CapEx」的对比，他的回应是：今天对比不公平，因为客户结构不同——对方几乎是全世界的代工，Intel 仍主要是 Intel 的代工；成为外部客户 foundry 后 CapEx 才会跟上来。

这个回应逻辑自洽，但也暴露战略悖论（整理者归纳）：

1. 要提高 CapEx 强度，需要更多外部客户晶圆；  
2. 要获得外部客户，需要已证明的 PDK / 良率 / 封装；  
3. 要证明这一切，又需要持续 CapEx 与学习晶圆。

溢出需求能缩短冷启动，但不能取消这个环。政策补贴若只建厂、不建 foundry 产品组织与客户成功团队，容易得到「漂亮的空洁净室」。Ranade 还提到制造业极度风险厌恶：没有 incumbent 愿意主动做可能停产一天的大胆实验——因为美元成本不可接受。这对「用试点革命改写制造」的外部想象是一盆冷水，却是内部理性。

关于「追赶 TSMC」他拆成多面：规模追赶是渐进的；工艺上要「在正确球园区且非常可预测」，并且不是单一晶体管指标，而是一族晶体管与产品组合。可预测性被反复强调——对 foundry 客户，迟到的惊喜不如准时的平庸。

## 四、与主流叙事的对齐与分歧

| 常见叙事 | 节目提供的修正 |
| --- | --- |
| GPU 荒 = Nvidia 产能不足 | 更深瓶颈在光刻/工具网络、良率学习与封装互连 |
| 节点数字决定胜负 | 良率闭环、PDK、可预测性同样决定客户敢不敢下单 |
| High-NA = 领先象征 | 取决于架构 ROI，不是勇气勋章 |
| 多花钱就能追上 TSMC | CapEx 与客户结构绑定；规模优势自我强化 |
| 3D 堆叠解决一切 | 逻辑热限制强制走向异构封装而非无限竖堆 |
| 建厂补贴 = 算力自主 | 工具配额、人才与 PDK 组织无法用剪彩代替 |
| 第二供应商很快分流订单 | 窗口存在，但只对「交得出、料号稳、文档齐」打开 |

## 五、对三类读者的行动启示

**1. 云与模型公司（需求方）**  
把供应链尽调从「哪家 GPU」扩展到「哪条封装路线、哪代互连、第二 foundry 的 PDK 成熟度与支持响应」。单点押注 TSMC 先进节点在节目描绘的世界里往往仍是理性选择，但也越来越贵；双源策略必须以工程可信度为门槛，而不是以新闻稿与参观照片为门槛。内部规划应显式建模「工具交期冲击」而不只是「晶圆厂名号」。

**2. 半导体、设备与封装投资者**  
关注工具交期、High-NA 实际插入节点、先进封装产能与 hybrid bonding 良率，而不是只跟踪晶圆厂 CapEx 指引数字。AI 需求抬高了设备商议价权，也把「年产量上限」变成宏观变量。对 Intel 叙事，区分「工艺演示进度」与「外部客户收入占比」两套仪表盘。

**3. 政策与主权算力推动者**  
建厂支票解决不了 EUV 配额与人才密度；更应追问：本地是否具备缺陷分析闭环、PDK 团队、封装能力，以及是否有真实客户晶圆来喂学习曲线。风险厌恶是制造侧的理性默认值，政策设计若假设工厂愿意为政治目标承受停产级实验，会与激励不相容。

## 六、这期没讲透、需要你自行补课的点

- **具体外部客户导入名单与 18A 设计 win** 未展开成可审计列表——精读不能代替订单与 tape-out 追踪。
- **与 Samsung foundry、以及特殊工艺（模拟、RF、成熟制程）** 的比较几乎缺席。
- **软件栈 / 编译器 / 通信库对 chiplet 架构的适配成本** 停留在互连物理层，未进入 CUDA 级生态讨论。
- **地缘政治与出口管制** 作为背景存在，但不是论证主轴；读者需自行叠加。
- **标题中的 2045** 更多是启发式时间尺度，节目并未给出严格的 2045 技术路线图预测模型。

## 七、与同周其他内容的交叉阅读建议

- 若你刚看完云厂商/CEO 谈「AI 需求无限、继续加码 CapEx」类访谈：用本期的工具与封装约束做对冲阅读，避免只活在需求曲线上。  
- 若你关注 agent/应用层爆发：记住应用层的「算力自由感」往往建立在制造层缓慢变量之上；产品节奏与晶圆节奏不是同一时钟。  
- 若你做中文科技媒体对「国产算力」的跟踪：把本期的五层约束（工具、良率、PDK、封装、CapEx–客户）当成检查清单，比单看参数海报更不容易自欺。

## 八、一句话收束

这期最有价值的不是「Intel 会不会赢」的答案，而是一张 **AI 时代半导体制造的约束地图**：工具网络、良率闭环、PDK 产品化、封装互连、CapEx–客户正反馈。把这五张图层叠在一起，再看任何「明年算力翻倍」「建厂即可自主」的预测，噪声会小很多；也更能理解为什么在 AI 软件叙事光速前进时，硬件供给仍像在地质时间里挪动。


## 九、收听与引用时的操作建议

精读之外，若你要二次传播或写内部简报，建议固定三段证据链，避免只摘金句：

1. **需求冲击段（开场 + 设备商旁白）**：用来回答「这是不是又一轮周期噪声」。把「40–50% 高于最大产能」与 AI 加速器挤占先进节点份额放在一起，比单独喊「GPU 缺货」更难被反驳。  
2. **良率/PDK 段（Auth）**：用来回答「第二供应商能不能用」。没有缺陷闭环速度与可交付 PDK，溢出订单不会自动掉进自家产线。  
3. **封装/CapEx 段（Osborn + Ranade）**：用来回答「性能下一跳在哪、钱该砸向哪」。节距演进与 CapEx–客户结构，比节点口号更能指导采购与投资尽调。

引用时请回到原片时间线与官方转写核对专有名词（14A、18A-P、Foveros、High-NA、PDK 等）；中文精读里的意译可能平滑了工程细微差别。若用于投资备忘录，务必单独验证最新客户导出口径与财报 CapEx，本解读截止于节目发布信息，不跟踪盘后新闻。

最后提醒：标题里的「2045」是启发式远景，不代表嘉宾给出了可审计的二十年路线图；把本期当「约束地图」使用，而不是当「未来时间表」使用，会更不容易误读。


对于只想带走最小行动项的读者：把「工具交期、良率闭环、PDK、封装节距、客户结构」写进下周的算力供需例会议程，比再多读一篇产业评论更有用。

transcript.md:
**Dwarkesh Patel:** There’s never been as big a shock to the semiconductor industry as the current surge in demand from AI.

**Gary Dickerson:** AI is driving incredible computing demand.

**Peter Wennink:** Easily 40-50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Progress in AI has been driven by
exponentially increasing compute
. To sustain that progress,
foundries
like Intel will need to manufacture far more leading-edge compute, both by producing more chips and by improving what each chip can do.
But the production of these chips is bottlenecked by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers. Most famously,
ASML
’s
EUV machines
.

**CNBC:** If they don’t have the equipment, they can’t make the chips here.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I spent two days touring Intel’s
fabs
to prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I’m joined by

**Chris Auth:** , who leads development of all the processes that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens. If
14A
is going to come out in three years or two years from now, what is happening from now till then?
I want you to walk me through as much detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the
yield
improving?” to what kind of
telemetry
you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run? I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.

**Chris Auth:** 14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage, so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now. Right now, we’re getting very close to where we’re finalizing the process. We’re finalizing the tool sets that it will be manufactured on, and we’re working on the fine-tuning of each of the process steps.
There are about 2,000 steps in the factory that you have to go do. You need to do really intricate work at each one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned, it can go into manufacturing, it can run thousands of wafers a week on this process, and it can be repeatable every single time.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Right now, you might have a certain yield. Walk me through how that increases month over month. There’s a line running at 14A. What happens from now till next month that will result in the yield changing? How do you identify where the defects are? How do you fix that?

**Chris Auth:** There’s a constant process that we go through in identifying defects. There are two main ways that we’ll identify them. One is we have
inline metrology
. We have tools that will look at the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.” Then also at the end of line, either
electrical test
or we sort and see where the fails are. We will identify failures, and then we will get analysis on those failures. We’ll cross-section it.
You were in the
TEM lab
yesterday, and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect, and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh, that defect is between these layers, so it must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section, which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”
What we’ve learned is that you don’t want to do too much innovation in one node, because the more innovation that you do, the more complex it becomes.
While you’ll be able to get that to work, you need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece. You’ve got to figure out how much innovation you can put in in order to meet the customer’s requirements in the timeline that they need it.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Intel learned how costly that tradeoff can be with delays to its
10 nanometer node
, whose original target launch date was 2016, but which didn’t begin manufacturing until 2018.

**Vivek Arya:** Usually Intel has been the keeper of
Moore’s Law
, a new cadence of manufacturing every two years, but their last set of products slipped almost four years.

**Yahoo Finance:** Intel today having its worst day in four months,
the stock now down more than 15%
. I also want to point out
Taiwan Semiconductor up 13% off of Intel’s bad news
.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Walk me through what lessons you think Intel has learned from 10 nanometer.

**Chris Auth:** Ten nanometer was a good example of where we had very aggressive targets. We were doing what was called hyperscaling at the time, so we were scaling much faster than what had been historically done. In order to do that, we came up with all sorts of innovative ideas on how we could achieve that without new tools, because the tools weren’t ready. That put a lot of burden on the process and a lot of burden on the engineers.
Now, at the end of the day, 10 nanometer is a great technology. It has world-class yield, it has world-class performance, it has world-class cost, but it took us longer to do that than what we would have liked. So we’ve tried to take that learning into future technology nodes and say, “Hey, we need to limit the amount of innovation we put in there to make sure that we keep it on schedule.”

**Dwarkesh Patel:** What do you think was the main technology that should’ve been saved for a future version?

**Chris Auth:** EUV was probably the big thing. When we started to define 10 nanometer, the conclusion was EUV was not ready.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** EUV is extreme ultraviolet
lithography
. It prints chip patterns with light at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers, about 14 times shorter than that emitted by
previous tools
that chipmakers had relied on. The shorter the wavelength, the finer the features that a single exposure can print.
But Intel decided this technology wasn’t going to be ready in time.
TSMC
transitioned to EUV much sooner. It
put EUV into volume manufacturing in 2019
and ramped it up further on its
5nm node
in 2020.
Intel’s first EUV process
did not reach products until 2023, so TSMC had about four more years of experience with these machines.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Yesterday, we were at the research lab getting a preview of 2D materials and
CFET
and
ruthenium interconnects
. I’m curious about how you decide whether that technology is mature enough for the next node.

**Chris Auth:** One thing that did also come out of 10 nanometer is we started to define a set of maturity metrics. We use those maturity metrics in a process which we call
phase gate
, where we would say, “To go from pathfinding into development, these are the criteria that we need to go hit.” There are yield criteria, defect criteria, performance criteria, and we need to hit those in order to move to the next set of the flow.
If there’s something that doesn’t make that, then it misses that, and it goes on to the next technology. We focus on the items that are ready and we can run and put into a process, because one of the key things is staying on schedule.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Staying on schedule is hard partly because new
transistor
designs take decades to mature. Modern chip transistors evolved from the
planar MOS transistor
, demonstrated in 1960. The history of transistors since has been the progression from two dimensions into three. Each development that Chris goes on to describe, from
FinFET
to
gate-all-around
, is a step in that progression. So it’ll help to first look at a basic transistor and how its parts have changed over time.
A transistor is basically a switch. When it’s turned on, it allows current to flow between its two ends, which are called the source and the drain. A piece called a gate sits on top of the silicon between the source and the drain. Applying a positive voltage to the gate turns the switch on, because the positive voltage pulls negatively charged electrons in the silicon beneath up toward the gate. However, a thin layer of insulation stops them from actually reaching the gate. So the electrons collect just beneath that insulation and form a thin conducting path from the source to the drain. This is called the channel. Remove the voltage and the electrons disperse, the channel disappears, and the switch turns off.
As transistors shrank, the source and the drain got so close together that current could flow through the channel even when the switch was supposed to be off. We needed a better way to control the channel and prevent current from leaking through.
The fix was to give the gate a tighter grip on the channel by touching it from more sides. In the original planar transistor, the gate only touches the channel from the top. The FinFET transistor squeezes the channel into a thin vertical fin of silicon. The gate drapes over the fin, so it controls the channel from three sides.
The next progression from there was to cover not only the top and the sides of the channel, but also the bottom. This technology is called gate-all-around, and it slices the channel into thin ribbons, each of which gets completely wrapped around by the gate.
But getting gate-all-around to work required new materials and new manufacturing steps. To build these floating ribbons of silicon, you first sandwich them between alternating layers of a
temporary placeholder material
, which holds the space where the gate will eventually go. We use a placeholder because the materials in the real gate wouldn’t survive the processing that comes after, which involves baking the wafer at around 1,000 degrees Celsius. Once these hot steps are done, chipmakers etch away the placeholder, leaving the ribbons suspended. Then they fill the gaps around every ribbon with a thin coat of a special insulator called a
high-k material
, whose purpose is to let the gate pull more strongly on the channel. And then on top of this material, they put the metal of the gate itself.
FinFET was demonstrated in a lab in 1989 and
reached volume production at Intel in 2011
. A gate-all-around transistor had been demonstrated a year earlier, in 1988, but
Samsung didn’t begin producing gate-all-around chips until 2022
. So these ideas, FinFET and gate-all-around, were developed around the same time, but they reached production a decade apart. I wanted to ask Chris why it took so long to get to this current gate-all-around technology.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Maybe you can walk me through the process of getting into high-volume manufacturing. I want to understand concretely, once you have an idea that, “Hey, we’re going to make the channel smaller, we’re going to surround it…” All the other problems of material science, figuring out how to not destroy the gate, how do they actually get figured out? Why does it take so long?

**Chris Auth:** Gate-all-around’s a good example, because back in the ’90s we knew of this idea. But we knew there were going to be these problems on how you put this into high-volume manufacturing. At the same time, there are other things like high-K metal gate. There’s
strained silicon
, there’s FinFETs that are out there. It’s a question of when’s the right time to go and tackle those?
Well, you don’t want to tackle something before you have to. If you have these other things that can drive performance, you would go and do that. So we went through this path. We did strained silicon, high-K metal gate, we did FinFETs, and then it became, “Well, we need to do things further. How do we get there?” Well, gate-all-around’s really the ultimate transistor out there. Maybe it’s time to go and start tackling some of those issues that you have. You’re right, now you have to look at how do you put high-K metal gate in with gate-all-around.
It’s that innovation that takes time. Sometimes you need new materials. Sometimes you need a different tool in order to be able to do some of the things that you need to go do, and that requires invention from the tool vendors. You have to go to the tool vendor and say, “Hey, I need a tool that can do XYZ. I need a gas that can deposit this particular material that goes into that. I need a heating chuck that has this characteristic to it.”
All those things take time. Some of it’s iterative, where you have to run a gate-all-around transistor and say, “Oh, well, that didn’t work. Let me figure out what was wrong with my hypothesis and try it again with some different structure.”

**Dwarkesh Patel:** How has the nature of R&D changed from the era of just making planar transistors smaller and smaller and getting the benefits of
Dennard scaling
, to the world we’re in today? Is it just a totally different kind of R&D process? Previously it was, “Let’s make things smaller, smaller, smaller.” Now you look at all these other facets of performance at the same time, and improvements in size don’t come as easily. Walk me through whether there was some crucial change in the R&D process at that point.

**Chris Auth:** If you look at the ’80s and ’90s, yes, it was driven really by Dennard scaling, lithography. We just made things smaller, transistors got faster, they got more reliable, and it was a very predictable cadence. When we started to hit the 2000s, we saw, “That’s not good enough anymore. We need to do something different.”
To me, it became this golden age of innovation. For each technology node, how are you going to provide more scaling? How are you going to provide more performance? It drove things like strained silicon. It drove high-K metal gate. It drove FinFETs. It drove gate-all-around. It drove
backside power
. These are things that in the ’80s and ’90s you would be like, “Oh no, we’re not touching any of that,” because we just continued to have the same process flow. We just scaled it, scaled it, scaled it.
But for somebody like me who’s a transistor junkie, it’s awesome, because now the playbook’s open. You can do all sorts of things out there. You can bring in new materials. Just look at the number of materials we used to use in the ’90s versus the materials today. It’s probably gone up 10X. There’s a lot of innovation. There’s
atomic layer deposition
. You’re controlling this stuff atom by atom. So it’s changed a lot how you approach the process. Before, it was, “Try to not change anything.” Now it’s, “Take the sledgehammer and start tearing the thing up and come up with some new idea.”

**Dwarkesh Patel:** For 14A, Intel is using a new kind of lithography machine:
High-NA EUV
. It uses the same extreme ultraviolet light as today’s EUV machines, but changes the optics. NA, or
numerical aperture
, is a measure of how wide a cone of light the machine’s mirrors can focus onto the wafer. The wider the cone you can focus, the smaller the spot that your light can carve. Standard EUV machines have an NA of 0.33. High-NA widens it to 0.55. So High-NA can print features about 1.7 times smaller in a single pass.
When features are smaller than the lithography machine can print, chipmakers have to split the pattern across several passes, each printing a different set of features. The most tightly packed patterns can require two, three, or even four passes.
Each additional pass takes up valuable time on a machine that costs around $200 million, and it introduces another opportunity for defects. High-NA machines cost about twice as much, but they can reduce the number of passes that are needed. So the question which determines whether they justify their higher price is how much more time they save and how much they reduce the risk of defects.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Now you guys are using High-NA EUV tools for 14A, whereas
TSMC has said that they don’t make economic sense yet for them
. How do you decide whether the next litho tool is the one that is ready to adopt or not?

**Chris Auth:** High-NA’s a good example of where, because of the architecture of our technology versus TSMC’s, we make different conclusions off of the same tool set. We use backside power. That means that you actually alleviate some of the pitch requirements you have on the front side. That allows you to print that directly with High-NA. TSMC has to run tighter pitches because they don’t have backside power, and they can’t do that with High-NA, so they have to use double patterning EUV.
So for them, it’s not very helpful. For us, it is very helpful. Now at 14A, we’ve left it as an option, and it’s something that we’ll have a discussion with the customer on, because there’s some value proposition to it, and there’s some complexity that it adds.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Chris is referring to a feature called backside power. A chip has two different kinds of wiring. Power lines deliver electricity to the transistors, and they need to be thick. Signal lines let the transistors talk to each other. They’re much thinner, but they need to be spaced apart so that the signal from one wire doesn’t interfere with the signal from another. In the past, all of these power lines and signal lines had to be crammed together on top of the transistors.
Intel’s newest process
moves these power lines below the transistors, to the back of the wafer

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Just to give the audience a sense of how big the AI demand is and how well it monetizes the products you guys are producing: you can crunch the numbers, and the numbers seem to suggest that just a couple billion dollars of CapEx on Intel’s account results in enough chips — or the logic for enough chips — to produce, say, $100 billion of revenue for the AI model companies.
Of course, there are so many other players within that stack. There’s also memory and other things. But it’s crazy that a couple billion dollars of CapEx, which can be amortized over many different years, produces $100 billion of revenue every single year. That seems to suggest that at some point that should percolate down. At some point, the AI labs could just say, “We’ll just buy everything. Produce as much as you can. We’ll guarantee future income streams.”

**Pushkar Ranade:** There are early signs that could actually be happening already. The demand signals are just so high. But I think you were alluding to how the value is accumulating at the top of the technology stack. What is essentially happening is we moved from a fully vertically integrated industry 30-40 years ago, maybe longer, to a very horizontal industry, where you have foundries, you have equipment makers, you have their suppliers.
Today, every
hyperscaler
is
designing their own chips
, and the scale of the hyperscalers is so large. Some of the model companies, for example, their demand is so high they could easily consume an entire fab’s worth of silicon on their own, or multiple fabs’ worth, and they definitely have the capital to fund that.
So in some sense, we are moving from a horizontal world again to a pseudo-vertical world. It’s not monolithically vertically integrated, but it’s kind of virtually vertically integrated.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** What is the nature of economies of scale in this business? If you look at how many wafers at the leading edge TSMC versus Intel is shipping, it’s upwards of 3X for TSMC. What kinds of advantages do you get at this point from economies of scale? Or is it that once you reach a certain point, the economies of scale get weaker?

**Pushkar Ranade:** That’s a very important question. This entire business just relies on economies of scale. If you look at all the advanced manufacturing companies out there, in semiconductor foundries the scale economics is probably the purest. The reason for that is the fixed cost is just so incredibly high. Once you build a fab, like 80% of your cost structure is fixed. What that means is every extra percentage of utilization is adding far more in revenue.
So it’s extremely important. We’ll fight for every extra percent of fab utilization, but also every extra percentage of fab output. Let’s say I’m making some wafers today and the yield is 60%. If I improve the process and the die yield becomes 65% or 70%, it’s not a linear advantage. I’m getting way more output for the given footprint. So there’s always room to improve the economies of scale.
That’s one of the reasons why you’re seeing so much
consolidation
in this business.
There are only three foundries left at the advanced node
for that exact reason. Along the way, many companies just stopped manufacturing. I don’t know if you’ve seen… There’s a chart where 40 years ago there were like 20 foundries. Over time the number of foundries kept diminishing until today there are only three.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** What is then the concrete master plan to catch up to TSMC? Even though TSMC is ahead, there’s so much overflow demand at their leading edge, where
N3
is now majority
AI accelerators
and maybe
majority Nvidia alone
. There’s all this demand for CPUs, for other things, which are also, by the way, needed for AI. There’s this
humongous influx in demand for CPUs because of AI
.
How do you see this opportunity right now, where Intel’s a few years behind, while TSMC is just way oversaturated?

**Pushkar Ranade:** Catching up to TSMC has multiple facets. The catch-up that we need to do is in scale. Like you said, they’re just a much larger wafer manufacturer today than we are, and even bigger than what Samsung is. Catching up in scale will be a gradual process.
If you meant catching up in terms of just the technology, I think we’re already there. We might be a few percent off on
performance or power or area
density. But this sort of benchmarking, where one foundry is ahead or one foundry is behind, makes sense when you’re a whole generation behind or two generations behind or ahead. That’s when it makes a meaningful difference in your die output or your die area or functionality like power. But if you’re within a few percent, you’re splitting hairs at that point in time, because it’s not very unidimensional. It’s not just about density, it’s not just about raw performance. Different applications require different vectors.
You can be off by a few percent, but you need to be on time. Your execution needs to be such that your yields are very high to support very large and very rapid ramps. That actually is more important than catching up on a few percent in performance or area.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I was looking at some
SemiAnalysis
numbers that seem to suggest that in terms of transistor density, 14A — which will come out in 2028 — would be comparable to
N2
.

**Pushkar Ranade:** First of all, I would dispute your benchmarking. But like I said, it’s important to be generally in the right ballpark and be very predictable. Also, it’s not unidimensional. We don’t build one type of transistor, let’s say 14A or 18A. You build a few different types of transistors. There’s a
low-leakage transistor
, there’s a high-performance, high drive current transistor.
You’re building
SRAMs
. There’s a high-density SRAM, there’s a high-performance SRAM. There are many other functionalities like analog circuits,
RF circuits
. It’s the sum of all of those that makes a technology competitive.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I guess that makes the CapEx you do right now even more important.
TSMC is on track to do around $50 billion in CapEx this year
. You’re
on track to do around $20 billion
. If the tools you’re buying right now will determine who can service all this crazy AI demand that’s coming up, it makes the difference in CapEx right now even more important, or for the US versus other countries.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Yes, very much. It’s a little bit of an unfair comparison between us and TSMC today, just because today they’re a foundry for basically everybody and we’re largely a foundry for Intel. We’ll become a foundry for others. In due course, our CapEx will also grow.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Intel started as a DRAM business in the late ’60s
. You guys were producing DRAM,
which you sold off
. A couple years ago,
you sold off your flash business
. Thoughts on that? For context for the audience, these are now multi-trillion-dollar industries because they’ve just exploded as a result of AI demand.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Clearly, in hindsight, probably not the smartest time to sell off a flash memory business. There were good reasons why we did that when we did. Clearly, nobody could see this enormous demand.
But today, the world will eat up as much compute as can possibly be made, and it’ll eat up as much memory as can possibly be made. I would argue that
the supply crunch is larger for memory
today than it is for compute.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Can I summarize what seems to me the takeaways from your projections? You can tell me if that’s correct. That marginal production can increase actually very fast — on the scale of 12 months — but the amount of increase up till the end of the decade is extremely limited. Production could be higher next year than what people are forecasting, but production in 2030 is not going to be significantly higher than what people are forecasting.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Unless the entire supply chain ramps up production very quickly. We’re already in the middle of ’26, so there’s not that many years until the end of the decade. Given the
lead times
… Let’s say you place an enormous order for tools today, and you’re looking at 18 months to get those tools. You’re already into basically ’28. From that point on, if you have to build a new shell, build a new fab, you’re basically looking at the end of the decade.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I think it’ll be interesting to discuss
the partnership you guys have
with
Elon
on
Terafab
. What’s going on there?

**Pushkar Ranade:** Well, Elon’s publicly talked about his desire to build a fab.

**Elon Musk:** We either build the Terafab or we don’t have the chips. And we need the chips, so we’re going to build the Terafab.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Sort of the same thinking. He’s seeing just an enormous increase in demand for silicon, for compute and for memory. I think he came to the conclusion that his own businesses are going to require a lot of silicon.
He thought maybe he should just do it all on his own. But unlike building a car, for example, this is such an intricate and complicated process that we thought we could work together to help accelerate his bringing up his fab.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** But because of the bottleneck at the tool level, it seems like the net amount of silicon in the world won’t increase. It’s just that maybe if somebody were to start a new fab, they would get access to guaranteed supply in a way that they wouldn’t have if they’re working with another person’s foundry.

**Pushkar Ranade:** It’s not just tools. A fab does require a lot of power,
a lot of water
, a lot of consumables. There are many other input variables as well.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** But those can be scaled in the way that tools cannot.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Some more than others, but yes. In one sense, yes, we need a lot more equipment. But it is true, we also just need a lot more raw fab space, raw
clean room
capacity.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** If you think of a foundry like Intel, which has to build these expensive facilities and buy expensive tools, I wonder what you think the economics of that fundamentally could look like, whether it could get more economical, whether it could scale faster.

**Pushkar Ranade:** Like I described earlier, this is an extremely capital-heavy business. If you just plot how much it costs to build a fab over the last 20, 30, 40 years, I think it’s
doubling every 4-5 years
. Even inside the fab, if you look at the cost to do lithography, which is the most expensive module — just patterning — that itself is doubling at more than that rate. Today,
a High-NA EUV scanner and all its associated equipment costs like $400 million
.
So what does that mean? If that rate were to continue, if you just draw the line, does that mean four years from now the cost of patterning is going to be like $800 million? It doesn’t really make sense.
A very interesting thought exercise is to ask, are there things that could be just very radically different that we could do today that we perhaps couldn’t do 20 years ago? This is a very risk-averse industry for very good reason, for exactly that reason. You put in tens of billions of dollars, and you really don’t want to take any risks. You want to keep doing things the way they’ve been done for literally decades.
This is not just true of semiconductors, but everything really. If you’ve just kept on doing that for decade upon decade, you just become indoctrinated. There are engineers who probably work at Intel who are new, who come in and they’re taught, “This is how the fab works, this is the process flow.” They just take that as gospel. That’s just how it is done. But is that really the best way to build a chip today? It’s a really valid question.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** I’m very curious what you’re hinting at, because it could be anything from figuring out ways to use fewer litho passes and economize on this expensive component, to maybe we need to rethink the transistor. What is the level of—

**Pushkar Ranade:** All of the above. Transistor architecture is evolving. Just the silicon transistor has continued to evolve over 30, 40 years, and that will continue. You’ve seen the evolution from the planar transistor to FinFETs to now gate-all-around transistors. There’ll be more. That roadmap exists, it’s pretty well defined, with a lot of people working on it.
But there are things like… Do you really need a clean room today? Do you need the infrastructure to be as sophisticated, as complex as it is today?

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Surely one can run an experiment where you have people eating hamburgers and smoking cigars in the research fab and see what happens to yield.

**Pushkar Ranade:** That would be a great experiment to run, but no incumbent — Intel or TSMC or Samsung — would want to willingly do that. That’s what I meant by this. It’s a very risk-averse business, for good reason. Every one day lost in productivity is… I don’t know how many dollars.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** But you save so much money in not having to build clean rooms in the future.

**Pushkar Ranade:** But it’s really the risk, the fear of the unknown. Nobody is going to willingly take that risk. That’s why I think sometimes it’s good to just start with a clean slate and rethink everything.
The same thing applies to chip design, by the way. Many of the ways we do CPU design were probably locked in 30 years ago. Does that mean it’s smart to still do it the same way? Probably not. But this is a very complex problem. In chip design, I guess the capacity to take risk is maybe higher. This one, less so. But given where the economics is today, I think it’s a very valid question to ask. Maybe there’s a smarter way to do this.

**Dwarkesh Patel:** To close out, maybe we’ll start off at the same question we began the interview with, which is, how does Intel respond to this crazy AI demand that’s incoming and has already arrived?
It sounds like what Intel ought to do — if the ultimate bottleneck is that you guys already have these foundries, you already have the ability to expand these foundries, but what you will eventually lack is the tools from upstream in the supply chain — is to just raise as much capital as possible right now. The same way that
Nvidia has locked down memory and other components for reportedly hundreds of billions of dollars worth of commitments
that it’s made, Intel should maybe do the same thing: make all these commitments so that over the coming years, the US is in good position to have the bulk of semiconductor manufacturing at the most advanced levels happening here.

**Pushkar Ranade:** You’re suggesting we should be buying a lot more tools, right?

**Dwarkesh Patel:** Yeah, because it sounds like otherwise in a couple years you’d just be in a position where you’re like, “Oh man, we could be making trillions of dollars right now, but all the tools are in
Taiwan
.”

**Pushkar Ranade:** Yes, that’s a very valid question. Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we’ll be investing more.

Progress in AI has been driven by

foundries

turns.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
turns.text:
I spent two days touring Intel’s
fabs
to prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.

turns.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
turns.text: I’m joined by

turns.speaker: Chris Auth
turns.text:
, who leads development of all the processes that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more concrete detail is how the development of a new process actually happens. If
14A
is going to come out in three years or two years from now, what is happening from now till then?
I want you to walk me through as much detail as you can, everything from the level of “how is the
yield
improving?” to what kind of
telemetry
you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run? I want to understand what is going to happen over the next two years as concretely as possible.

turns.speaker: Chris Auth
turns.text:
14A has been in development for about three-plus years at this stage, so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to get it to the stage that it’s at right now. Right now, we’re getting very close to where we’re finalizing the process. We’re finalizing the tool sets that it will be manufactured on, and we’re working on the fine-tuning of each of the process steps.
There are about 2,000 steps in the factory that you have to go do. You need to do really intricate work at each one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned, it can go into manufacturing, it can run thousands of wafers a week on this process, and it can be repeatable every single time.

turns.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
turns.text: Right now, you might have a certain yield. Walk me through how that increases month over month. There’s a line running at 14A. What happens from now till next month that will result in the yield changing? How do you identify where the defects are? How do you fix that?

turns.speaker: Chris Auth
turns.text:
There’s a constant process that we go through in identifying defects. There are two main ways that we’ll identify them. One is we have
inline metrology
. We have tools that will look at the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.” Then also at the end of line, either
electrical test
or we sort and see where the fails are. We will identify failures, and then we will get analysis on those failures. We’ll cross-section it.
You were in the
TEM lab
yesterday, and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect, and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh, that defect is between these layers, so it must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section, which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”
What we’ve learned is that you don’t want to do too much innovation in one node, because the more innovation that you do, the more complex it becomes.
While you’ll be able to get that to work, you need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece. You’ve got to figure out how much innovation you can put in in order to meet the customer’s requirements in the timeline that they need it.

turns.speaker: Dwarkesh Patel
turns.text:
Intel learned how costly that tradeoff can be with delays to its
10 nanometer node
, whose original target launch date was 2016, but which didn’t begin manufacturing until 2018.

turns.speaker: Vivek Arya
turns.text:
Usually Intel has been the keeper of

turns.speaker: Yahoo Finance
turns.text:
Intel today having its worst day in four months,
the stock now down more than 15%
. I also want to point out
